Source: http://www.drugabuse.gov

Posted October 16, 2000
(MarijuanaNews note: NIDA not only bought itself a great little bit of prohibitionist propaganda, and distributed it on an embargoed basis to the major news outlets that did their usual job as parrots for the prohibitionists, NIDA even paid the PR Newswire to distribute to everyone else.
See
Media Alert: Watch for New NIDA Study Claiming Animal Tests Prove Marijuana Is Addictive. Great Marketing of Prohibitionist Propaganda.

Bush says that he will double NIDA’s budget, so, if he wins, buy PRNewswire stock and move to Canada. If Gore wins, then just move to Canada.

This study involved putting little

squirrel monkeyson IV-feeds, showing them how to get cocaine, which they started self-administering, and then replacing the cocaine with a saline solution. They stopped dosing themselves, when the coke stopped. Then the monkeys were given the same routine, but with a water-soluble synthetic analogue of THC. They resumed self-administering the pseudo-THC at roughly the same levels as cocaine.

This proves that adult human beings must be arrested for using whole smoked cannabis, because failure to do so would send the wrong message to adolescent squirrel monkeys that shooting up synthetic THC is harmless. Or something like that.

There are several problems here.

First, locking social animals like squirrel monkeys in a cage and tying them to an IV-feed must place them under enormous stress. [Where is PETA when we really need them?] Consequently, extrapolating from that situation to normal human use, or even normal monkey use, is highly questionable. However, that may explain why marijuana is so popular in prisons, where it seems to be very common. Of course, if NIDA has its way, there will be so many more people in prison that this may be of increasing relevance.

See
" Mandatory Prison Drug Testing May Have Perverse Effect " -
Discouraging Cannabis; Encouraging Hard Drugs. - London Times

Second, in one AP version, the researcher is quoted as saying that the monkeys did not show any sign of being sedated, so this raises questions about the similarity of the effect of THC on humans and squirrel monkeys.

As it happens, there is government approved clinical evidence that THC is not addictive in humans. Remember synthetic THC is an FDA/DEA approved drug.


See
No Evidence That THC Is Addictive Says Maker of Marinol
After 9 Month Study Including Law Enforcement

Of course, the humans were not injecting THC. No one does, except lab monkeys.

In fact, the biggest problem with the stated conclusions is the claim that injecting a THC analogue in monkeys -- or even humans -- proves something about the addictiveness of whole marijuana as used by humans.

Whenever the prohibitionists argue against any use of marijuana, they make much of the fact that there are more than 60 cannabinoids in whole cannabis. Here they choose to ignore that fact. Marijuana and THC are not the same things. Many patients dislike Marinol precisely because it is not the same as whole smoked marijuana in its effect.


See
Gettman Petition For Hearings On Marinol Rescheduling Uses DEA’s Own Arguments Against It.
Why Marinol Is Not Medical Marijuana. Wonderfully Brilliant!

In short, this study proves nothing about marijuana, but a lot about NIDA and the media.

The New York Times ran an AP story with the headline: " Marijuana Seen as Addictive in Monkeys. " The LA Times ran the story under the header: " Center Labels Pot Addictive After Test Monkeys Take Repeated Doses. " Never mind that the monkeys were not getting marijuana.)

FOR RELEASE, October 15, 2000

NIDA News Release Contact: Beverly Jackson or Michelle Muth 301-443-6245

NIDA Researchers Find That Animals Exposed to Marijuana's Active Component Will Self-Administer the Drug

Scientists at the National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA) have demonstrated that laboratory animals will self-administer marijuana's psychoactive component, THC (delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol), in doses equivalent to those used by humans who smoke the drug.

Self-administration of drugs by animals, long considered a model of human drug-seeking behavior, is characteristic of virtually all addictive and abused drugs.

" This study is simple and its findings are clear, " says NIDA Director Dr. Alan I. Leshner.

" Animals will work to get THC. This emphasizes further the similarity between marijuana and other abusable, addicting substances. Both animals and humans will work to acquire access to marijuana in the same way that both animals and humans change their behavior to get other drugs of abuse, like cocaine and heroin. "
See
Is marijuana addictive?
and
The Need For Drug Prohibition Education.
Analysis By Richard Cowan.
How Can Parents Tell Their Children The Truth In A Sea Of Lies About Marijuana?
and links

Dr. Steven Goldberg and colleagues at NIDA's Intramural Research Program in Baltimore, Maryland, report in the current issue of Nature Neuroscience that squirrel monkeys will self-administer intravenous injections of THC.
(MarijuanaNews note: Nature Neuroscience is a peer-reviewed journal, which says nothing about NIDA’s interpretation.)

" This is the first study in which it has been possible to show that monkeys or other research animals will self-administer THC. There are many factors which may explain this behavior, including the fact that in our study we used doses of THC that are directly comparable to doses in marijuana smoke inhaled by humans, " Dr. Goldberg says.
(MarijuanaNews note: Cross-specie extrapolations are always questionable, but that is the least of the problems with this report.)

Before the study began, the scientists first established self-administration behavior in squirrel monkeys that received repeated intravenous injections of cocaine after pressing a lever 10 times for each injection.At the start of the study, the researchers replaced cocaine with saline solution and the animals' self-administration stopped. When saline was replaced with THC in a solution that would rapidly pass from blood to the brain, the animals resumed self-administration, rapidly pressing the lever to obtain on average 30 injections of THC during each of a series of 1-hour sessions.

Treatment with a compound that prevented THC from binding to cannabinoid receptors on brain cells almost completely eliminated self-administration of THC, but had no effect in another group of monkeys self-administering cocaine under identical conditions, according to Dr. Goldberg.

" The drug-seeking behavior in these animals was comparable in intensity to that maintained by cocaine under identical conditions, and was obtained from a range of doses comparable to those self-administered by humans smoking a single marijuana cigarette, " Dr. Goldberg says. " This finding suggests that marijuana has as much potential for abuse as other drugs of abuse, such as cocaine and heroin. "
(MarijuanaNews note: This finding suggests that Dr. Goldberg will have no problem getting his next NIDA grant. One AP story reports, " Goldberg said that does not necessarily mean marijuana is as addictive as cocaine in people. " Now he can have his academic respectability and his NIDA check, too.

How nice, something for everyone.)

The National Institute on Drug Abuse is a component of the National Institutes of Health, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. NIDA supports more than 85 percent of the world's research on the health aspects of drug abuse and addiction.
(MarijuanaNews note: That is the only important fact in this press release.)

The Institute carries out a large variety of programs to ensure the rapid dissemination of research information and its implementation in policy and practice. Fact sheets on the health effects of drugs of abuse and other topics can be ordered free of charge in English and Spanish from NIDA Infofax at 1-888-NIH-NIDA (644-6432) or 1-888-TTY-NIDA (889-6432) for the deaf.
